claim: Nutrient availability within the tumor microenvironment can influence cancer progression, therapeutic response, and metastasis.
source: Nutrient availability within the tumor microenvironment (TME) can influence cancer progression, therapeutic response, and metastasis (Muir and Vander Heiden, 2018; Muir et al., 2017; Abbott et al., 2023; Cantor et al., 2017; Vande Voorde et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2016; Gui et al., 2016; Ferraro et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2020; Ngo et al., 2020; Faubert et al., 2020; Rossiter et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: A comprehensive analysis of what nutrients are found in cancer tissue interstitial fluid, and how this deviates from nutrients available in the corresponding normal tissue, has not been conducted.
source: How metabolite availability is regulated in the TME has been a topic of extensive research (Apiz Saab and Muir, 2023; Sullivan et al., 2019; Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017; Sullivan and Vander Heiden, 2019; Reinfeld et al., 2021); however, a comprehensive analysis of what nutrients are found in cancer tissue interstitial fluid, and how this deviates from nutrients available in the corresponding normal tissue, has not been conducted.
evidence: Statement about the absence of prior comprehensive analysis

claim: Whether global tumor nutrient availability is actively modified by tumor cells, the accompanying immune, endothelial, and stromal cells, or predominantly influenced by the conditions of the originating resident tissue, is not known.
source: Thus, whether global tumor nutrient availability is actively modified by tumor cells, the accompanying immune, endothelial, and stromal cells, or predominantly influenced by the conditions of the originating resident tissue, is not known.
evidence: Statement about lack of knowledge regarding determinants of tumor nutrient availability

claim: A number of distinct types of primary renal cancers, driven by a diverse set of genetic programs, arise from the kidney.
source: Notably, a number of distinct types of primary renal cancers, driven by a diverse set of genetic programs, arise from the kidney (Linehan et al., 2010; Linehan, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on renal cancer types

claim: Quantitative polar metabolomics measured 104 metabolites in RCC patient samples.
source: We isolated interstitial fluid from RCC tumors (TIF) and from adjacent non-tumor bearing kidney tissue (KIF), then performed quantitative polar metabolomics (n = 104 metabolites) and lipidomics (n = 210 metabolites) of these fluids alongside plasma collected from patients with kidney cancer at the time of nephrectomy (Figure 1A; Supplementary files 1–3).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of metabolites measured in the study

claim: Lipidomics measured 210 metabolites in RCC patient samples.
source: We isolated interstitial fluid from RCC tumors (TIF) and from adjacent non-tumor bearing kidney tissue (KIF), then performed quantitative polar metabolomics (n = 104 metabolites) and lipidomics (n = 210 metabolites) of these fluids alongside plasma collected from patients with kidney cancer at the time of nephrectomy (Figure 1A; Supplementary files 1–3).
evidence: Direct statement of the number of lipids measured in the study

claim: Principle component analysis of polar and lipid metabolite levels revealed that TIF and KIF principally clustered distinctly from plasma.
source: Principle component analysis (PCA) of polar and lipid metabolite levels measured in these samples revealed some differences between TIF and KIF, but these tissue analytes principally clustered distinctly from plasma (Figure 1B,C), highlighting that the nutrients found in circulation differ extensively from those found in tissue interstitial fluid.
evidence: PCA analysis results showing distinct clustering patterns

claim: The nutrients found in circulation differ extensively from those found in tissue interstitial fluid.
source: Principle component analysis (PCA) of polar and lipid metabolite levels measured in these samples revealed some differences between TIF and KIF, but these tissue analytes principally clustered distinctly from plasma (Figure 1B,C), highlighting that the nutrients found in circulation differ extensively from those found in tissue interstitial fluid.
evidence: Interpretation of PCA results showing distinct clustering

claim: Lipid features were tightly concordant between KIF and TIF, in contrast to plasma where lipid components have widespread variation.
source: In particular, lipid features were tightly concordant between KIF and TIF, in contrast to plasma where lipid components have widespread variation.
evidence: Observation from lipidomics analysis comparing tissue and plasma samples

claim: Clear cell RCC is the most common subtype of RCC.
source: We also performed PCA of polar and lipid metabolite levels measured in material derived from the subset of patients with clear cell RCC (ccRCC), as this is the most common subtype of RCC (Linehan, 2012; Muglia and Prando, 2015) and represented the largest fraction of the patient samples available for analysis.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on RCC subtypes

claim: Similar clustering patterns for ccRCC metabolite levels were found as those found when analyzing data collected from all patient-derived material.
source: We found similar clustering patterns for ccRCC metabolite levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) as those found when we analyzed the data collected from all patient-derived material.
evidence: Comparison of PCA results between ccRCC subset and all patients

claim: Levels of most polar metabolites do not significantly differ between TIF and KIF.
source: Further analysis by t- and chi-squared tests revealed that levels of most polar metabolites do not significantly differ between TIF and KIF (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Statistical analysis results comparing TIF and KIF polar metabolites

claim: Differences in lipid composition between TIF and KIF were fewer than when comparing the lipid composition of either TIF or KIF compartments to plasma.
source: These same analyses revealed a difference in the number of statistically different metabolites when comparing TIF and KIF lipid composition, but these differences were fewer than when comparing the lipid composition of either TIF or KIF compartments to plasma (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Statistical analysis results comparing lipid composition across sample types

claim: Metabolites found in TIF and KIF are largely similar based on measurable analytes.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that metabolites found in TIF and KIF are largely similar based on these measurable analytes, although there are individual polar and lipid metabolites that differ between TIF and KIF (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Summary interpretation of statistical analyses and PCA results

claim: The human RCC tumor nutrient environment is primarily driven by factors shared with kidney tissue, rather than being extensively modified by cancer cells or other factors unique to the tumor.
source: These data support the notion that the human RCC tumor nutrient environment is primarily driven by factors shared with kidney tissue, rather than being extensively modified by cancer cells or other factors unique to the tumor.
evidence: Interpretation of the similarity between TIF and KIF metabolite profiles

claim: 2-hydroxyglutarate levels are elevated in TIF compared to KIF.
source: Focusing on differences between TIF and KIF using data derived from the entire patient dataset, we found several metabolites to be elevated in TIF compared to KIF that agree with known metabolic characteristics of RCC. These include increased levels of 2-hydroxyglutarate (Shim et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021), kynurenine (Wettersten et al., 2015; Ganti et al., 2012; Lucarelli et al., 2017), and glutathione (Wettersten et al., 2015; Hakimi et al., 2016; Figure 2C), all consistent with prior reports and known biology of RCC.
evidence: Measured metabolite levels in TIF vs KIF, consistent with prior research

claim: Kynurenine levels are elevated in TIF compared to KIF.
source: Focusing on differences between TIF and KIF using data derived from the entire patient dataset, we found several metabolites to be elevated in TIF compared to KIF that agree with known metabolic characteristics of RCC. These include increased levels of 2-hydroxyglutarate (Shim et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021), kynurenine (Wettersten et al., 2015; Ganti et al., 2012; Lucarelli et al., 2017), and glutathione (Wettersten et al., 2015; Hakimi et al., 2016; Figure 2C), all consistent with prior reports and known biology of RCC.
evidence: Measured metabolite levels in TIF vs KIF, consistent with prior research

claim: Glutathione levels are elevated in TIF compared to KIF.
source: Focusing on differences between TIF and KIF using data derived from the entire patient dataset, we found several metabolites to be elevated in TIF compared to KIF that agree with known metabolic characteristics of RCC. These include increased levels of 2-hydroxyglutarate (Shim et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021), kynurenine (Wettersten et al., 2015; Ganti et al., 2012; Lucarelli et al., 2017), and glutathione (Wettersten et al., 2015; Hakimi et al., 2016; Figure 2C), all consistent with prior reports and known biology of RCC.
evidence: Measured metabolite levels in TIF vs KIF, consistent with prior research

claim: Glucose is depleted in TIF compared to plasma.
source: Of note, we observed depletion of glucose and elevation of lactate in TIF compared to plasma, again consistent with known increases in glucose fermentation to lactate in this tumor type (Kaushik et al., 2022; Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Kaelin, 2008; Courtney et al., 2018; Sanchez and Simon, 2018; Figure 2D).
evidence: Measured glucose levels in TIF vs plasma, consistent with prior research

claim: Lactate is elevated in TIF compared to plasma.
source: Of note, we observed depletion of glucose and elevation of lactate in TIF compared to plasma, again consistent with known increases in glucose fermentation to lactate in this tumor type (Kaushik et al., 2022; Masson and Ratcliffe, 2014; Kaelin, 2008; Courtney et al., 2018; Sanchez and Simon, 2018; Figure 2D).
evidence: Measured lactate levels in TIF vs plasma, consistent with prior research

claim: The levels of glucose and lactate measured in TIF were similar to those measured in KIF.
source: However, the levels of glucose and lactate measured in TIF were similar to those measured in KIF, arguing that glucose was not further depleted in TIF compared to KIF (Figure 2D).
evidence: Comparison of measured glucose and lactate levels between TIF and KIF

claim: Glucose was not further depleted in TIF compared to KIF.
source: However, the levels of glucose and lactate measured in TIF were similar to those measured in KIF, arguing that glucose was not further depleted in TIF compared to KIF (Figure 2D).
evidence: Interpretation of glucose measurements in TIF vs KIF

claim: The average glucose concentration in RCC TIF is near or above the threshold identified as limiting for proliferation in a range of cancer cell lines.
source: These data challenge the notion that cells in the TME are necessarily glucose starved (Burgess and Sylven, 1962; Gullino et al., 1964; Hirayama et al., 2009; Urasaki et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2015), as the average glucose concentration is near or above the threshold identified as limiting for proliferation in a range of cancer cell lines (Birsoy et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparison of measured glucose levels to published proliferation thresholds

claim: While glucose availability is reduced in the TME relative to blood, it is not completely depleted.
source: Regardless, these findings fit with other data from RCC, as well as from other tumor types, demonstrating that while glucose availability is reduced in the TME relative to blood, it is not completely depleted (Sullivan et al., 2019; Reinfeld et al., 2021; Siska et al., 2017).
evidence: Interpretation of glucose measurements consistent with prior research

claim: VHL loss in ccRCC leads to increased HIF1α-driven expression of glucose transporters and glycolytic enzymes.
source: This finding is somewhat unexpected, given that VHL loss in ccRCC leads to increased HIF1α-driven expression of glucose transporters and glycolytic enzymes (Linehan et al., 2010; Wettersten et al., 2015; Hakimi et al., 2016; Mandriota et al., 2002; Semenza, 2009; Rathmell et al., 2018), but exchange of glucose between blood and interstitial fluid may be sufficient to prevent glucose depletion to levels that are less than those found in normal kidney tissue.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on VHL loss and HIF1α

claim: Exchange of glucose between blood and interstitial fluid may be sufficient to prevent glucose depletion to levels that are less than those found in normal kidney tissue.
source: This finding is somewhat unexpected, given that VHL loss in ccRCC leads to increased HIF1α-driven expression of glucose transporters and glycolytic enzymes (Linehan et al., 2010; Wettersten et al., 2015; Hakimi et al., 2016; Mandriota et al., 2002; Semenza, 2009; Rathmell et al., 2018), but exchange of glucose between blood and interstitial fluid may be sufficient to prevent glucose depletion to levels that are less than those found in normal kidney tissue.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed glucose levels

claim: Evidence for increased glucose metabolism in some forms of human RCC is evident from [¹⁸F]Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-positron emission tomography scans.
source: Indeed, evidence for increased glucose metabolism in some forms of human RCC is evident from [¹⁸F]Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-positron emission tomography scans (Reinfeld et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2012); however, FDG-glucose uptake is variable in the more common ccRCC subtye and can display regional variation (Brooks et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior FDG-PET imaging studies

claim: FDG-glucose uptake is variable in the more common ccRCC subtype and can display regional variation.
source: Indeed, evidence for increased glucose metabolism in some forms of human RCC is evident from [¹⁸F]Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-positron emission tomography scans (Reinfeld et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2012); however, FDG-glucose uptake is variable in the more common ccRCC subtye and can display regional variation (Brooks et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on FDG uptake variability

claim: In vivo tracing studies of isotope-labeled glucose have demonstrated distinct metabolic fluxes in ccRCC tumors compared to matched adjacent kidney tissue at the time of surgery.
source: In vivo tracing studies of isotope-labeled glucose have demonstrated distinct metabolic fluxes in ccRCC tumors compared to matched adjacent kidney tissue at the time of surgery (Courtney et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior isotope tracing study

claim: ccRCC silences the key gluconeogenic enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1.
source: Lastly, these data are notable with respect to the finding that ccRCC silences the key gluconeogenic enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (Li et al., 2014), as it suggests that loss of gluconeogenesis in cancer cells has minimal effect on local glucose availability.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on FBP1 silencing

claim: Loss of gluconeogenesis in cancer cells has minimal effect on local glucose availability.
source: Lastly, these data are notable with respect to the finding that ccRCC silences the key gluconeogenic enzyme fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (Li et al., 2014), as it suggests that loss of gluconeogenesis in cancer cells has minimal effect on local glucose availability.
evidence: Inference from glucose measurements in context of known FBP1 silencing

claim: Arginine is depleted to very low levels in murine pancreatic cancer TIF.
source: Recent studies have found that arginine is depleted to very low levels in murine pancreatic cancer TIF (Sullivan et al., 2019; Apiz Saab et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2023), a phenomenon facilitated by myeloid-derived arginase activity (Apiz Saab et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on arginine depletion in pancreatic cancer

claim: Arginine depletion in murine pancreatic cancer TIF is facilitated by myeloid-derived arginase activity.
source: Recent studies have found that arginine is depleted to very low levels in murine pancreatic cancer TIF (Sullivan et al., 2019; Apiz Saab et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2023), a phenomenon facilitated by myeloid-derived arginase activity (Apiz Saab et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on arginase activity

claim: Arginine is not significantly depleted in KIF or TIF from RCC patients compared to plasma.
source: Of note, arginine is not significantly depleted in KIF or TIF from RCC patients compared to plasma, although levels of related urea cycle metabolites are reduced in TIF and KIF compared to plasma (Figure 2E).
evidence: Measured arginine levels in RCC samples

claim: Levels of related urea cycle metabolites are reduced in TIF and KIF compared to plasma.
source: Of note, arginine is not significantly depleted in KIF or TIF from RCC patients compared to plasma, although levels of related urea cycle metabolites are reduced in TIF and KIF compared to plasma (Figure 2E).
evidence: Measured urea cycle metabolite levels in RCC samples

claim: Myeloid cell infiltrates in RCC are not sufficient to lower arginine levels.
source: These findings suggest that myeloid cell infiltrates in RCC are not sufficient to lower arginine levels, and this observation may relate to the responsiveness of RCC to T-cell immune checkpoint blockade therapy (Santoni et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference from arginine measurements and comparison to pancreatic cancer

claim: The observation that arginine is not depleted in RCC may relate to the responsiveness of RCC to T-cell immune checkpoint blockade therapy.
source: These findings suggest that myeloid cell infiltrates in RCC are not sufficient to lower arginine levels, and this observation may relate to the responsiveness of RCC to T-cell immune checkpoint blockade therapy (Santoni et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative connection between arginine levels and immunotherapy response

claim: Primary RCC tumors commonly downregulate ASS1 expression and urea cycle activity.
source: These data are also notable with respect to the observation that primary RCC tumors commonly downregulate ASS1 expression and urea cycle activity (Yoon et al., 2007; Perroud et al., 2009; Ochocki et al., 2018; Khare et al., 2021), implying that the amount of arginine in KIF or TIF is sufficient to support cancer cell proliferation without the requirement for de novo arginine synthesis involving ASS1 upregulation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on ASS1 downregulation

claim: The amount of arginine in KIF or TIF is sufficient to support cancer cell proliferation without the requirement for de novo arginine synthesis involving ASS1 upregulation.
source: These data are also notable with respect to the observation that primary RCC tumors commonly downregulate ASS1 expression and urea cycle activity (Yoon et al., 2007; Perroud et al., 2009; Ochocki et al., 2018; Khare et al., 2021), implying that the amount of arginine in KIF or TIF is sufficient to support cancer cell proliferation without the requirement for de novo arginine synthesis involving ASS1 upregulation.
evidence: Inference from arginine measurements in context of known ASS1 downregulation

claim: Metastatic kidney cells in the lung upregulated ASS1 expression due to the lower availability of arginine in the lung compared to the kidney.
source: To this point, a recent study found that metastatic kidney cells in the lung upregulated ASS1 expression due to the lower availability of arginine in the lung compared to the kidney (Sciacovelli et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on metastatic kidney cells

claim: Distinctive lipid metabolism alterations are associated with RCC.
source: Given that distinctive lipid metabolism alterations are known to be associated with RCC (Heravi et al., 2022; Gebhard et al., 1987; Saito et al., 2016; Riscal et al., 2021; Valera and Merino, 2011), we probed our lipidomics dataset to investigate changes in lipid composition within RCC TIF compared to KIF and plasma.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on RCC lipid metabolism

claim: Cholesterol levels in both TIF and KIF were notably lower when compared to plasma.
source: We found cholesterol levels in both TIF and KIF were notably lower when compared to plasma (Figure 2F), aligning with prior studies observing a roughly fivefold depletion of VLDL, LDL, and HDL cholesterol in tissue interstitial fluid versus plasma (Vessby et al., 1987; Dabbagh and Frei, 1995; Parini et al., 2006).
evidence: Measured cholesterol levels consistent with prior research

claim: Prior studies observed a roughly fivefold depletion of VLDL, LDL, and HDL cholesterol in tissue interstitial fluid versus plasma.
source: We found cholesterol levels in both TIF and KIF were notably lower when compared to plasma (Figure 2F), aligning with prior studies observing a roughly fivefold depletion of VLDL, LDL, and HDL cholesterol in tissue interstitial fluid versus plasma (Vessby et al., 1987; Dabbagh and Frei, 1995; Parini et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on cholesterol in tissue vs plasma

claim: There is a roughly threefold elevation in cholesterol and cholesteryl esters in TIF compared to KIF.
source: Although cholesterol levels were dramatically lower compared to plasma, we did detect a roughly threefold elevation in cholesterol and cholesteryl esters in TIF compared to KIF (Figure 2G,H), which is intriguing given work showing ccRCC suppresses de novo cholesterol biosynthesis leading to a dependence on exogenous cholesterol import to meet metabolic demands (Riscal et al., 2021).
evidence: Measured cholesterol and cholesteryl ester levels in TIF vs KIF

claim: ccRCC suppresses de novo cholesterol biosynthesis leading to a dependence on exogenous cholesterol import to meet metabolic demands.
source: Although cholesterol levels were dramatically lower compared to plasma, we did detect a roughly threefold elevation in cholesterol and cholesteryl esters in TIF compared to KIF (Figure 2G,H), which is intriguing given work showing ccRCC suppresses de novo cholesterol biosynthesis leading to a dependence on exogenous cholesterol import to meet metabolic demands (Riscal et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on cholesterol metabolism in ccRCC

claim: Alterations in local lipid metabolism may be a feature of RCC to supply cancer cells with elevated cholesterol in the TME.
source: These findings may argue that alterations in local lipid metabolism may be a feature of RCC to supply cancer cells with elevated cholesterol in the TME and raises questions about the dynamic regulation of cholesterol metabolism involving non-cancer cells in these tumors.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of cholesterol measurements

claim: Intermediates in nucleotide metabolism were different between RCC plasma and healthy plasma or NSCLC plasma.
source: Lastly, we examined the composition of plasma from the RCC patients undergoing nephrectomy, and compared the polar metabolite levels to polar metabolite levels in plasma collected from healthy adult donors, and to polar metabolites levels in plasma from non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D). Among the metabolites analyzed, intermediates in nucleotide metabolism stood out as being different between samples.
evidence: Comparison of metabolite levels across different plasma samples

claim: Cystine concentration was approximately twofold higher in plasma from patients with RCC compared to levels in plasma from healthy individuals.
source: Cystine concentration was also noted to be approximately twofold higher in plasma from patients with RCC compared to levels in plasma from healthy individuals based on the measurements here and available data from the Human Metabolome Database (HMDB; Wishart et al., 2022; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Measured cystine levels compared to HMDB data

claim: There are influences from the tumor on the composition of nutrients in the circulating plasma.
source: This finding demonstrates that there are influences from the tumor on the composition of nutrients in the circulating plasma.
evidence: Inference from differences in plasma metabolites between RCC patients and healthy individuals

claim: Cystine levels have been demonstrated to influence sensitivity to glutaminase inhibitors.
source: The cystine finding was specifically notable because cystine levels have been demonstrated to influence sensitivity to glutaminase inhibitors (Muir et al., 2017), and RCC was a tumor type that showed early responses in glutaminase inhibitor clinical trials (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on cystine and glutaminase inhibitors

claim: RCC was a tumor type that showed early responses in glutaminase inhibitor clinical trials.
source: The cystine finding was specifically notable because cystine levels have been demonstrated to influence sensitivity to glutaminase inhibitors (Muir et al., 2017), and RCC was a tumor type that showed early responses in glutaminase inhibitor clinical trials (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior clinical trial data

claim: The concentration of cystine in RCC plasma was comparable to that of NSCLC plasma.
source: The concentration of cystine in RCC plasma was comparable to that of NSCLC plasma, which suggests this may be a more common feature of tumor physiology than previously appreciated.
evidence: Comparison of measured cystine levels between RCC and NSCLC plasma

claim: Elevated cystine in cancer patient plasma may be a more common feature of tumor physiology than previously appreciated.
source: The concentration of cystine in RCC plasma was comparable to that of NSCLC plasma, which suggests this may be a more common feature of tumor physiology than previously appreciated.
evidence: Inference from similarity of cystine levels in RCC and NSCLC plasma

claim: There was a 1.6-fold increase in circulating cystine in the fasted state compared to the fed state in a healthy donor.
source: To explore this further, we collected fed and fasted plasma from a healthy donor and found a 1.6-fold increase in circulating cystine in the fasted state compared to the fed state (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Measured cystine levels in fed vs fasted plasma from one donor

claim: Fasting status may partially explain the higher cystine concentration in RCC or NSCLC plasma.
source: This observation offers a plausible explanation for at least a component of the higher cystine concentration in RCC or NSCLC plasma, but a larger trial, including plasma from non-fasted cancer patients, would be needed to verify whether cystine levels are affected by fasting status.
evidence: Inference from fasted vs fed cystine measurements

claim: Therapies influenced by nutrient levels, such as glutaminase inhibitors, may be influenced in part by a patient's diet or fed/fasted state.
source: Moreover, the observed rise in cystine concentration due to fasting raises an intriguing possibility that therapies influenced by nutrient levels, such as glutaminase inhibitors (Muir et al., 2017), may also be influenced in part by a patient's diet or fed/fasted state (Wilinski et al., 2019; LaBarre et al., 2021), which could have effects on therapeutic efficacy.
evidence: Speculative connection between fasting-induced cystine changes and therapy efficacy

claim: The metabolites found in RCC TIF differ from those reported in mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) TIF.
source: To this end, it is notable that the metabolites found in RCC TIF differ from those reported in mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) TIF (Sullivan et al., 2019; Apiz Saab et al., 2023), and from those found in interstitial fluid derived from mouse brain and mammary fat pad tissue (Ferraro et al., 2021).
evidence: Comparison of RCC TIF metabolites to published data from other tumor types

claim: The metabolites found in RCC TIF differ from those found in interstitial fluid derived from mouse brain and mammary fat pad tissue.
source: To this end, it is notable that the metabolites found in RCC TIF differ from those reported in mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) TIF (Sullivan et al., 2019; Apiz Saab et al., 2023), and from those found in interstitial fluid derived from mouse brain and mammary fat pad tissue (Ferraro et al., 2021).
evidence: Comparison of RCC TIF metabolites to published data from other tissues

claim: Analysis of PDAC TIF from tumors implanted in different tissue sites noted differences in metabolite levels.
source: Findings from analysis of PDAC TIF from tumors implanted in different tissue sites also noted differences in metabolite levels (Sullivan et al., 2019), supporting the notion that cancer must adapt to a specific tissue nutrient environment rather than determine the majority of nutrients present.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on PDAC in different tissue sites

claim: Cancer must adapt to a specific tissue nutrient environment rather than determine the majority of nutrients present.
source: Findings from analysis of PDAC TIF from tumors implanted in different tissue sites also noted differences in metabolite levels (Sullivan et al., 2019), supporting the notion that cancer must adapt to a specific tissue nutrient environment rather than determine the majority of nutrients present.
evidence: Inference from comparison of metabolite levels across different tumor types and tissues

claim: Each tissue represents a unique nutrient environment driven by interactions between resident non-cancer cell types.
source: These findings may suggest that each tissue represents a unique nutrient environment driven my interactions between resident non-cancer cell types, with potential implications for cancer metastasis.
evidence: Inference from tissue-specific metabolite profiles

claim: Accessing a tissue nutrient environment that shares features with the primary cancer site may be needed to support proliferation of metastatic cancer cells.
source: That is, this model raises the possibility that accessing a tissue nutrient environment that shares features with the primary cancer site is needed to support proliferation of metastatic cancer cells, and may contribute to the stereotyped pattern of metastases associated with cancers arising in specific tissues (Riihimäki et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative model connecting tissue nutrient environments to metastasis patterns

claim: Tissue-specific nutrient environments may contribute to the stereotyped pattern of metastases associated with cancers arising in specific tissues.
source: That is, this model raises the possibility that accessing a tissue nutrient environment that shares features with the primary cancer site is needed to support proliferation of metastatic cancer cells, and may contribute to the stereotyped pattern of metastases associated with cancers arising in specific tissues (Riihimäki et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculative connection between nutrient environments and metastasis patterns

claim: Tissue-specific nutrient environments may present a challenge for therapies targeting nutrient dependencies in patients with metastatic tumors.
source: These findings may also present a challenge for therapies targeting nutrient dependencies in patients with metastatic tumors given that available metabolites could differ in each organ of metastasis.
evidence: Speculative implication of tissue-specific nutrient environments for therapy

claim: Quantification of steady-state nutrient levels does not directly reflect nutrient use.
source: Quantification of steady-state nutrient levels does not directly reflect nutrient use, as nutrient consumption and release rates cannot be derived from these steady-state measurements.
evidence: Statement about limitations of steady-state measurements

claim: An increase in levels of a metabolite in tissue relative to blood must represent some local production in the tissue.
source: An increase in levels of a metabolite in tissue relative to blood must represent some local production in the tissue, while a decrease in the levels of a metabolite relative to blood must represent some local consumption, however a lack of change does not mean a metabolite is not involved in metabolism in that tissue.
evidence: Logical inference about metabolite level changes

claim: A decrease in the levels of a metabolite in tissue relative to blood must represent some local consumption.
source: An increase in levels of a metabolite in tissue relative to blood must represent some local production in the tissue, while a decrease in the levels of a metabolite relative to blood must represent some local consumption, however a lack of change does not mean a metabolite is not involved in metabolism in that tissue.
evidence: Logical inference about metabolite level changes

claim: A lack of change in metabolite levels does not mean a metabolite is not involved in metabolism in that tissue.
source: An increase in levels of a metabolite in tissue relative to blood must represent some local production in the tissue, while a decrease in the levels of a metabolite relative to blood must represent some local consumption, however a lack of change does not mean a metabolite is not involved in metabolism in that tissue.
evidence: Statement about limitations of interpreting steady-state measurements

claim: The levels of at least some of the metabolites measured in normal kidney may have been affected by the nearby tumor, or the fact that the patient had a cancer.
source: Moreover, that KIF was collected from non-tumor renal tissue in specimens that were resected from patients with RCC raises the possibility that the levels of at least some of the metabolites measured in normal kidney were affected by the nearby tumor, or the fact that the patient had a cancer.
evidence: Acknowledgment of potential confounding factor in KIF measurements

claim: Analysis of interstitial fluid will not take into account local variation in nutrient levels across different tissue regions.
source: Additionally, we also note that analysis of interstitial fluid will not take into account local variation in nutrient levels across different tissue regions (Pan et al., 2016; Okegawa et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2022a; Miller et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022b).
evidence: Statement about limitation of bulk interstitial fluid analysis

claim: Microenvironmental differences will be averaged in the pooled collection method employed in this study.
source: Microenvironmental differences will be averaged in the pooled collection method employed in this study.
evidence: Statement about limitation of the collection methodology

claim: Known tumor heterogeneity, including the presence of both cancer and non-cancer cell types, are likely to drive gradients in nutrient availability within tumors.
source: Known tumor heterogeneity, including the presence of both cancer and non-cancer cell types, are likely to drive gradients in nutrient availability within tumors (Morandi et al., 2016; Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on tumor heterogeneity

claim: The processing methodology employed to collect interstitial fluid may itself lead to some cell lysis and release of intracellular metabolites.
source: Lastly, the processing methodology employed to collect interstitial fluid may itself lead to some cell lysis and release of intracellular metabolites, which would affect the measured metabolite concentrations.
evidence: Acknowledgment of potential methodological limitation

claim: Metabolite levels measured in one cancer type cannot necessarily be extrapolated to reflect which nutrients are found in the TME of other tumors.
source: The findings also emphasize that metabolites levels measured in one cancer type cannot necessarily be extrapolated to reflect which nutrients are found in the TME of other tumors.
evidence: Inference from differences in metabolite profiles across tumor types

claim: Fresh RCC tumors and matched healthy tissue were surgically removed from 55 patients.
source: Fresh RCC tumors and matched healthy tissue were surgically removed from 55 patients.
evidence: Statement of study sample size

claim: All metabolite samples were collected in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki principles under a protocol approved by the VUMC Institutional Review Board (protocol no. 151549).
source: All metabolite samples were collected in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki principles under a protocol approved by the VUMC Institutional Review Board (protocol no. 151549).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval

claim: Informed consent was received from all patients before inclusion in the study.
source: Informed consent was received from all patients before inclusion in the study.
evidence: Statement of informed consent procedures

claim: 51 metabolites were quantitated using the internal standard method.
source: 51 metabolites were quantitated using this internal standard method (see Supplementary file 2 for the metabolites quantitated with internal standards).
evidence: Statement of quantification methodology

claim: 53 metabolites were quantitated using external calibration.
source: Fifty-three metabolites were quantitated using this method.
evidence: Statement of quantification methodology

claim: The study included 55 TIF samples, 46 KIF samples, and 27 plasma samples for polar metabolite analysis.
source: Data represent 55 TIF, 46 KIF, and 27 plasma samples.
evidence: Statement from Figure 1B legend describing sample numbers

claim: The study included 34 TIF samples, 25 KIF samples, and 18 plasma samples for lipid analysis.
